Lessons.Title: Find the Area of Figures with Missing Sides
ExplanationParagraphs: Find the Area of Figures with Missing Sides: not every side length needs to be printed. Use the rectangular structure of a right-angled figure to match horizontal spans and vertical spans. Find the missing lengths from the known measurements, then split into non-overlapping rectangles, multiply side lengths and add their areas. A length needs a linear unit; area needs a square unit.

Warm-up — Mystery Sides: notice and wonder about the centimeter figure, think quietly, then discuss with a partner. The full top is 10 cm and the bottom right-hand leg is 4 cm wide, so the inside horizontal side is 10 − 4 = 6 cm. The full right height is 9 cm and the upper bar is 2 cm high, so the inside vertical side is 9 − 2 = 7 cm. Explain which horizontal or vertical parts make the same total. We can find the area even though these two labels began as question marks.

The Mystery Side: Tyler claims that the missing meter length is 5 m because it looks longer than the 4 m sides. Disagree with that reasoning. A drawing’s appearance cannot determine a measurement. The full vertical height is 12 m, made from the upper 6 m segment and the missing lower segment. Therefore 12 − 6 = 6 m, and 6 + 6 = 12 m checks it. Think quietly, compare with a partner, and explain how opposite-side relationships support the subtraction.

Practice with Mystery Sides — Figure A: use the same meter figure. Independently find its area. A horizontal split gives a top rectangle 8 m by 6 m and a lower-right rectangle 4 m by 6 m. Their areas are 48 m² and 24 m², so the whole covers 72 m². A vertical split gives a 4 m by 6 m left block and a 4 m by 12 m right block, again 24 + 48 = 72 m². Do not add the side labels as if they were areas.

After independent work, first find someone who used your method and explain why it makes sense. Then compare with someone who used a different method. Restate the partner’s method using “I heard you say …”; the original speaker may agree or clarify. Be ready to explain that method to the class (MLR8 Discussion Supports). Use timers, previews or transition reminders if helpful. Actual dialogue is reviewed by the teacher.

Figure B: work with your current partner on the foot-labelled T-shaped figure. The top width is 7 ft. The left overhang is 3 ft and the right overhang is 2 ft, so the missing stem width is 7 − 3 − 2 = 2 ft. The stem’s opposite vertical sides match, so its missing left side is 4 ft. Both upper bar sides are 2 ft. Label the missing lengths before using them in an area expression.

For Figure B, a horizontal split gives (7 × 2) + (2 × 4) = 14 + 8 = 22 ft². A three-rectangle method gives (3 × 2) + (2 × 6) + (2 × 2) = 6 + 12 + 4 = 22 ft²: left overhang, full-height center and right overhang. Each part covers a different region, so the bar is not counted twice. A valid method may need different missing lengths; explain which your method uses and how you found them.

Lesson synthesis: return to the warm-up figure. Explain how opposite sides of rectangles make corresponding horizontal totals and vertical totals agree. Once missing lengths are known, choose a non-overlapping partition and write the multiplication-and-addition expression that matches it. The section summary repeats these ideas: area is additive, and rectangular structure helps recover missing measurements. The summary drawing repeats the centimeter warm-up; it is not a new meter or foot problem.

New Edulytics Cool-down: the separate centimeter figure has a top width of 9 cm, an upper bar height of 2 cm, a total right height of 7 cm and a lower-right leg width of 3 cm. Find the missing inside horizontal and vertical lengths, then its area. The lengths are 9 − 3 = 6 cm and 7 − 2 = 5 cm. A horizontal split gives (9 × 2) + (3 × 5) = 18 + 15 = 33 cm². A vertical split gives (6 × 2) + (3 × 7) = 12 + 21 = 33 cm². Explain and label the parts. This independent assessment does not reproduce the publisher-gated Mystery Side Area Cool-down.

Optional centers: Five in a Row: Multiplication, stage 2 (factors 1–9), supports area calculations. Five in a Row: Addition and Subtraction, stage 8 (add within 1,000 with composing), is supporting practice. Invite a strategy from a student whose reasoning has not yet been heard. Teachers review the inferred sides, labelled drawings, expressions, alternative methods and actual discussion; typing a correct length or area is only a numerical anchor.

KeyConcepts.Title: Use rectangular structure
KeyConcepts.Definition: Matching opposite sides creates equal total horizontal or vertical spans.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Subtract known parts from the full span, keeping the same unit.

KeyConcepts.Title: Separate length from area
KeyConcepts.Definition: A length is measured along an edge; area measures covered squares.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use cm, m or ft for lengths and corresponding square units for areas.
KeyConcepts.Example: A missing side is 6 m; Figure A covers 72 m².

KeyConcepts.Title: Find only the missing measurements your method needs
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different partitions use different side lengths.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Draw the split and identify every rectangle’s two side lengths.
KeyConcepts.Example: Figure B stem width is 7 − 3 − 2 = 2 ft.

KeyConcepts.Title: More than one partition works
KeyConcepts.Definition: Disjoint parts cover the same original region.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply each part’s side lengths and add every part once.
KeyConcepts.Example: For Figure B, 14+8 and 6+12+4 both give 22 ft².

WorkedExamples.Title: Centimeter warm-up
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the two missing sides.
WorkedExamples.Method: Match complete horizontal and vertical spans.
WorkedExamples.Check: Use the printed labels, not a ruler on the screen.

WorkedExamples.Title: Critique Tyler’s claim
WorkedExamples.Question: Is the missing meter side 5 m because it looks longer than 4 m?
WorkedExamples.Answer: Disagree; the missing side is 6 m.

WorkedExamples.Title: Figure A area
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the meter figure’s area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Split into top bar and lower-right leg.

WorkedExamples.Title: Figure B area
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the missing sides and area of the foot figure.
WorkedExamples.Method: Recover stem dimensions, then choose non-overlapping parts.
Steps: Stem left side equals right side:4 ft.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Stem 2 ft by 4 ft; area 22 ft².

WorkedExamples.Title: New Edulytics assessment
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the new centimeter figure’s missing sides and area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Deciding the missing side from how long it looks.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The drawing’s apparent size is not a numerical justification.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use equal horizontal or vertical spans from rectangular structure.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtracting a horizontal length from a vertical total.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Match horizontal parts to horizontal totals and vertical parts to vertical totals.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 5+6 is 11, not the given full height 12.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using 7−3=4 ft for the stem width.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This forgets the right overhang of 2 ft.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Including the top bar again in the stem area.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The overlapping region would be counted twice.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use stem height below the bar, or separate three disjoint rectangles.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Entering 72 m for area or 6 m² for a side.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Linear units and square units describe different quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write 6 m for the side and 72 m² for Figure A area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correct number as proof of partner explanation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source asks students to compare and restate another method.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show the labelled split and have the teacher review the explanation and actual interaction.

SummaryPoints: Use rectangular structure to find missing lengths from matching spans.
Warm-up missing sides:6 cm and 7 cm.
Tyler’s missing side is 6 m, supported by 12−6, not by appearance.
Figure A area 72 m²; Figure B missing sides 2 ft and 4 ft, area 22 ft².
Two or three non-overlapping rectangles can represent the same figure.
Use linear units for lengths and square units for areas.
Compare and restate different methods; teacher reviews drawings and actual dialogue.
